entry.title: Rotom: A Microcontroller-Oriented Tweakable Block Cipher Using Modular Multiplication
entry.summary: Rotom: A Microcontroller-Oriented Tweakable Block Cipher Using Modular Multiplication (Full Version) IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper proposes Rotom, a family of 128-bit tweakable block ciphers designed for efficient software use on 32-bit microcontrollers. It uses modular multiplication as its main source of nonlinearity, with a fixed 16-bit S-box, a recursive linear layer, a compact tweakey schedule, and modular-addition key mixing. The authors compute the S-box's transition probabilities exhaustively to derive explicit differential and linear characteristic bounds. On ARM Cortex-M3 and M4, Rotom's cycle counts are close to Speck and well below MSX.

entry.title: A complete addition formula for twisted Edwards curves, a cryptographic curve family
entry.summary: Complete Addition Law for Twisted Edwards Curves IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026The paper constructs complete addition formulas in extended coordinates for twisted Edwards curves, valid for every pair of rational points under specified conditions. It analyses the exceptional fibres using a difference morphism and gives full and mixed evaluation schedules. The authors compare operation costs across cases, and state that doubling cost does not depend on the choice of coefficient. ★★★★ Notable: The authors construct complete addition laws for twisted Edwards curves, characterize exceptional fibres, prove existence over odd finite fields, and report operation costs.

entry.title: Communication complexity of secure MPC from a random oracle, including quantum variants
entry.summary: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the communication complexity of information-theoretically secure multi-party computation when only symmetric-key assumptions are available, modeled as a random oracle. For MPC with preprocessing, the authors prove that the known lower bound still holds in this model, so a random oracle cannot reduce online communication. For honest-majority MPC they give an Ω(|C|) lower bound and a matching construction for degree-2 polynomials, including inner products, when n = O(log λ). The paper also analyzes protocols that use quantum communication or a quantum-accessible random oracle. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend MPC communication lower bounds to the random oracle model, match them with a degree-2 construction, and study quantum communication savings and their costs.

entry.title: Tight depth lower bounds for amplifying pseudorandom generator stretch
entry.summary: Tight Depth Lower Bounds for Stretch Amplification IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies the depth overhead of stretch amplification for pseudorandom generators in the black-box model. It shows that black-box constructions with d adaptive phases satisfy an upper bound on output length M, implying the standard repeated-composition amplification is essentially optimal. The results also yield tight depth lower bounds for black-box PRF constructions from PRGs. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give tight depth lower bounds for black-box stretch amplification of PRGs, extending to PRFs, Avoid, and an oracle separation.

entry.title: Recovering master keys from the WBSLT white-box AES design by quotienting redundant lookup tables
entry.summary: Quotienting Redundant Tables: Practical Master-Key Recovery from WBSLT White-Box AES IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper is a cryptanalysis of WBSLT, a white-box AES design presented at NDSS 2026. It shows that the joint output of first-round TypeII lookup tables has an exact 16 × 16 quotient, which reveals the nibble partition of each AES input byte. Using public tables and traces of chosen encoded inputs, the authors report recovering the master key in the tested instances. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors use an exact quotient of public lookup tables to recover WBSLT white-box AES master keys, reporting full recovery across 200 general instances and variants.

entry.title: Cryptanalysis of MinRank 2.0: Reassessing Attacks on the MinRank Problem
entry.summary: Cryptanalysis of MinRank 2.0 IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper revisits attacks on MinRank, the hard problem underlying several post-quantum schemes such as the Mirath signature and multivariate schemes like UOV and MAYO. The authors improve the kernel-search attack, lowering its cost by 3 to 6 bits on Mirath parameters and solving Courtois challenge D, open since 2001. They also show that existing complexity estimates for the Kipnis–Shamir attack are inaccurate and give corrected figures. Finally, they extend the Support-Minors and Minors modelings with field equations, which lowers their estimates over small fields. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors improve kernel-search MinRank attacks, report solving open Courtois challenge D, and correct Kipnis-Shamir complexity estimates affecting several post-quantum schemes.

entry.title: The Fairest of Them All: Fair Leader Election Secure Under Two Corruption Models
entry.summary: The Fairest of Them All: Best-of-Both-Worlds Fair Leader Election IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how to pick a random leader fairly from n parties. It introduces best-of-both-worlds (BoBW) fairness: a small number of corrupt parties cannot bias the result, and a larger number still cannot improve their collective chances or reduce any honest party's chances. The authors present a protocol for t_S + t_GT < n, prove it optimal via a generalization of Cleve's impossibility, and give a protocol for the perfect-security setting. ★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce a new best-of-both-worlds fairness notion, give a protocol, and report a matching optimality proof with a generalized Cleve impossibility.

entry.title: Leakage-tolerant secure computation without leakage-free setup
entry.summary: Leakage-Tolerant Computation without Leakage-Free Setup IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies leakage-tolerant multi-party computation, where leakage from honest parties' internal states reveals no more than their inputs and outputs already do. In a computational model assuming only augmented non-committing encryption, the authors show that every adaptively well-formed functionality admits a semi-honest leakage-tolerant protocol without leakage-free preprocessing or a common reference string. Under the decisional Diffie-Hellman assumption, this extends to malicious security in the CRS model for all deterministic functionalities. In the information-theoretic setting, secure erasure enables statistically secure protocols for arbitrary functionalities when fewer than half the participants are maliciously corrupted. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show semi-honest leakage-tolerant MPC from augmented non-committing encryption alone, without leakage-free preprocessing or CRS, plus information-theoretic results and impossibilities.

entry.title: Keeping secrets safe from physical leaks by refreshing matrices
entry.summary: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how to protect secret data from side-channel attacks, where a device leaks partial information about its internal state. The secret is split into two vectors held by separate parts of the implementation, and it is refreshed by multiplying one share by a uniform invertible matrix and the other by its inverse. The authors prove this refresh remains secure under continual local leakage and give bounds on statistical distance. They also present a Boolean-circuit compiler with a privacy error bound, and formalize these results in Lean 4. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a matrix-refresh scheme for two-party shares with a statistical bound under continual local leakage, plus a circuit compiler.

entry.title: The Cost of Agreement in Secure Multiparty Computation
entry.summary: The Price of Agreement in Secure Multiparty Computation IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies secure multiparty computation (MPC) when a dishonest majority of parties may be corrupted, where output delivery cannot be guaranteed and protocols settle for security with abort. It focuses on unanimous abort, where either all honest parties receive output or all abort. The authors prove that for t ≤ n−2 corruptions, unanimous-abort broadcast and hence UA-MPC require at least t/(2(n−t)) rounds in expectation, matching the asymptotic bound for broadcast without abort. Consequently, expected-constant-round UA-MPC is possible if and only if a constant fraction of parties is honest. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove UA-broadcast and UA-MPC need at least t/(2(n-t)) expected rounds, answering an open question with a tight bound matching Dolev-Strong.

entry.title: Differential Cryptanalysis of SPEEDY: Revised Security Evaluation and Improved Key Recovery
entry.summary: Differential Cryptanalysis of SPEEDY: Revised Security Evaluation and Improved Key Recovery Attack IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper re-evaluates the resistance of the low-latency block cipher SPEEDY against differential cryptanalysis. The authors propose a search method based on search patterns that imposes no structural restrictions, using computational pruning and a conservative evaluation over the global space. For 4 rounds, the minimum number of active S-boxes is narrowed to [33,34], and the highest-probability differential characteristics known for 2 to 5 rounds are presented. The authors also optimize a prior key recovery attack, yielding the best known attack on SPEEDY-7-192. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a search-pattern method removing structural restrictions, improving bounds and reporting stronger characteristics and a key recovery attack on SPEEDY.

entry.title: Hardness of TFNP Classes in the Random Oracle Model
entry.summary: TFNP in the Random Oracle Model IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper examines which major TFNP classes are hard in the random oracle model. It shows that PPAD is hard on average in this setting, which together with known PLS hardness yields average-case hardness for EoPL. It also shows that UEoPL can be solved with polynomially many queries by an unbounded solver, and begins studying separations between TFNP subclasses. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors prove PPAD is average-case hard in the random oracle model, resolving a long-standing open problem and separating EoPL from UEoPL.

entry.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: Post-quantum pseudorandomness in TC⁰ from worst-case lattice hardness
entry.summary: Information Loss Is All You Need: TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026The paper introduces the learning with algebraic rounding (LAR) assumption, which replaces LWE's random noise with an explicit deterministic integer rounding map. Its pseudorandomness is based on quantum worst-case lattice problems such as GapSVP and SIVP. The authors use this to construct the first post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in TC⁰. They also show hardness of learning two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a learning-with-algebraic-rounding assumption, derive a post-quantum TC⁰ weak PRF from worst-case lattice hardness, and report hardness for learning two-hidden-layer ReLU networks.

entry.title: Power-analysis attack study on SHA-2-based SLH-DSA signatures
entry.summary: Correlation Power Analysis on SHA-2-Based SLH-DSA IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper applies non-profiled correlation power analysis to the address-based pseudorandom function of SLH-DSA across all six SHA-2 parameter sets, targeting SHA-256 compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. Experiments on an STM32F303 ARM Cortex-M4 used 30 secret seeds with 5,000 power traces per seed. Reported rates are conditional stage-wise results with preceding secret values supplied correctly, not end-to-end seed recovery rates. The authors conclude that side-channel protection must cover both compression rounds and message-schedule expansion. ★★★★ Notable: The authors report a staged non-profiled correlation power attack on SHA-2 SLH-DSA, covering compression rounds and message schedule, evaluated on an STM32F303 Cortex-M4.

entry.title: Complete Addition on Short Weierstrass Curves Using Point-Free Lines
entry.summary: Complete Addition on Short Weierstrass Curves with Point-Free Lines IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies addition formulas for short Weierstrass elliptic curves over fields. It gives coordinate changes and a complete Bosma–Lenstra addition law based on lines with no rational points on the curve, and proves such lines exist over every finite field of the stated characteristic. The paper also provides computational costs for several normalized families, complete doubling formulas, and applies a five-product identity to published Hessian addition formulas.

entry.title: Efficient hardware multiplier designs for ML-KEM on small FPGAs
entry.summary: Efficient Polynomial Multiplier Architectures for ML-KEM on Resource-Constrained FPGAs IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents two hardware architectures for polynomial arithmetic in Kyber, covering NTT, inverse NTT, and point-wise multiplication. One design uses a single processing element to save area, while the other uses two for higher throughput. Both target the modulus q = 3329 and avoid dedicated DSP blocks and BRAMs. The dual-PE design reportedly achieves the lowest area-time product and highest frequency among the compared designs.

entry.title: Kaiburr: ML-KEM Scaled to Higher Security Levels
entry.summary: Kaiburr: ML-KEM at (much) higher security IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines how to scale ML-KEM to higher security levels of the underlying MLWE problem. The authors note that simply increasing the module rank hits a limit set by decryption failure probability, so they generalize the noise distribution. They define three high-security parameter sets called Kaiburr and report benchmarks on 64-bit Intel CPUs and the Pavona silicon framework's coprocessor.

entry.title: FixSampZ: A Fixed-Point, Hardware-Efficient Sampler for Falcon Signatures
entry.summary: FixSampZ: A Fixed-Point Hardware-Efficient Discrete Gaussian Sampler for Falcon Signatures IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents FixSampZ, a hardware design for the SamplerZ component of the Falcon post-quantum signature scheme that uses no floating-point arithmetic. Implemented on an UltraScale+ FPGA, it matches all 1,024 official test vectors and uses 38% fewer LUTs, 21% fewer FFs, and 36% fewer DSPs than a floating-point baseline, with 21% fewer cycles at a higher clock frequency. The authors also report that replacing the ChaCha20 pseudorandom generator with Ascon-XOF128 saves a further 2 to 3 times in hardware resources with no added sampling latency.

entry.title: Certified radix-code design for finite-batch q-ary OT extension in private lookup
entry.summary: Finite-Batch q-ary OT Extension for High-Arity Private Lookup: Certified Radix--Code Co-Design IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the finite-batch design space of the CCG q-ary oblivious transfer extension family and derives certified radix-selection rules. For q=2^r, it formulates radix-code selection as a security-constrained discrete optimization problem and derives communication thresholds and lower bounds via the Griesmer bound. The framework is instantiated with simplex and BCH constructions, and the selected δ=12 codes are verified with Magma.

entry.title: Perseus: A Full-Stack Toolkit for Running AI Models on Encrypted Data
entry.summary: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents Perseus, a free and open Python library for running AI models on encrypted data, covering the cryptographic backend, data packing, encrypted nonlinear operations, and end-to-end model execution. It adds optimizations at each layer of the stack and reports state-of-the-art latency across several models, with accuracy and perplexity within 3% of plaintext models. For single-token decoding on Llama-3-8B, it is reported to be 3.96 times faster than any other implementation.

entry.title: PS-BKZ: Separating Outer Propagation and Local Processing in BKZ Lattice Reduction
entry.summary: PS-BKZ: Decoupling Outer Propagation and Local Processing in BKZ by Parameter Separation IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper systematically studies parameter separation in Block Korkine–Zolotarev (BKZ) lattice reduction, proposing a framework that uses separate parameters for outer propagation and local computation. It presents idealized and executable constructions in which an inner BKZ with a smaller blocksize supplies local vectors for larger outer blocks. For dimensions at least 200, experiments show lower mean root-Hermite factors and 14.1%–59.3% shorter mean running times than BKZ 2.0.

entry.title: Dual Coppersmith: Recovering Small Roots Without Solving Polynomial Systems
entry.summary: Dual Coppersmith: Finding Small Roots Without Multivariate Polynomial Systems IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper introduces Dual Coppersmith, a method for finding a small hidden root of modular polynomial equations. Instead of solving auxiliary polynomial systems, it embeds the hidden root as a short vector in a modular orthogonal lattice and recovers its direction with LLL, then reads the root from coordinate ratios. Experiments on the approximate common divisor and Herrmann-May problems support the model's predictions and show root recovery in higher-dimensional cases where the Gröbner-based baseline times out.

entry.title: Quadrinomials with high nonlinearity that are differentially 2^t-uniform
entry.summary: Differentially 2^t-uniform quadrinomials with high nonlinearity IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines cryptographic properties of a family of quadrinomials built as a generalization of a known family of APN quadrinomials. The authors show that the family is differentially 2^t-uniform over F_{2^n} and has the same Walsh spectrum as the Gold power function x^{2^t+1}. The paper also considers whether this family yields permutations.

entry.title: Challenge binding in FRESCO SPDZ2k: a message-level case study of predictable MAC-check seeds
entry.summary: Challenge Binding in FRESCO SPDZ2k: A Message-Level Case Study IACR ePrint · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines the SPDZ2k implementation in the FRESCO framework, where batched MAC-check coefficients come from a predictable public seed set at setup. The authors show through a message-level test that a specific deviation in value shares makes the recorded sum and product outputs violate a required relation, while the test framework still reports normal completion. They also assess a four-file candidate mitigation, but a complete mitigation argument is not presented.

entry.title: Apparent Timing Leaks on Cortex-M4: ML-KEM Decapsulation Evaluation
entry.summary: Phantom Timing Leaks on Cortex-M4: A Pre-registered Evaluation of ML-KEM Decapsulation IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This pre-registered study uses dudect-style fixed-versus-random timing tests to evaluate nine PQM4 ML-KEM decapsulation implementations on an STM32F411 (Cortex-M4). Invalid ciphertexts showed no detected timing difference, while fresh valid ciphertexts flagged all nine implementations with differences of 4 to 15 cycles. Matched-control and A/A tests suggest that these few-cycle differences can arise from the measurement harness alone, and the authors also found a functional bug in the ML-KEM-1024 m4fstack implementation.

entry.title: MODDIV-WC: A Public-Key Encryption Candidate Using Unit-Anchored Hankel Rounding
entry.summary: MODDIV-WC: Unit-Anchored Toeplitz/Hankel Rounding with Exact Binary-LWE Masking and an IND-CCA Security Route IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026The paper proposes MODDIV-WC, a public-key encryption and key-encapsulation candidate built on a widened Hankel map followed by integer division, along with an implicit-rejection Fujisaki–Okamoto wrapper. The authors argue IND-CCA security in the classical random-oracle model by combining one-way chosen-plaintext security with a modular Fujisaki–Okamoto analysis. The work explicitly makes no claims of practical 128-bit parameters, QROM security, or deployment.

entry.title: Efficient bucket sets for power-of-two radices in LFG-based MSM algorithms
entry.summary: Practical Optimal Bucket Sets with Power-of-Two Radices for LFG-Based MSM Algorithms IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper addresses multi-scalar multiplication (MSM), a key computation in pairing-based SNARK proof generation. For the Luo–Fu–Gong (LFG) framework, it presents two bucket set constructions for power-of-two radices q=2^c, using multiplier sets {1,2,3} and {1,3}. Both constructions asymptotically reach the counting bound q/(2|M|) and allow radix digits to be extracted efficiently with shifts and masks.

entry.title: An Efficient Decryption Failure Probability Estimator for LWE Encryption and Its Use in IBE
entry.summary: An efficient Failure Probability Estimator for LWE-based encryption, and application to IBE IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper designs a more efficient estimator for decryption failure probability in LWE-based encryption, implemented in C and CUDA C++ to handle higher parameters used in real structured-LWE schemes. The authors apply it to two Identity-Based Encryption schemes. For the first, the tool reduces ciphertext size by about 20%. For the second, it lowers the failure probability without changing key or ciphertext size.

entry.title: A note on making ring switching zero knowledge: an extension of Diamond and Posen's technique
entry.summary: A note on zero-knowledge ring switching IACR ePrint · Nov 4, 2026This paper makes the ring-switching technique of Diamond and Posen zero knowledge, resolving a problem left open in the literature. Over F_{2^n}, the technique uses n-1 auxiliary masks and n-1 quadratic constraints. These constraints are checked in zero knowledge by the underlying commitment scheme.

entry.title: Provable fast algorithms for exact shortest vector and approximate closest vector problems on random q-ary lattices
entry.summary: Fast Provable Algorithms for Approximate CVP and Exact SVP on Random q-ary Lattices IACR ePrint · Nov 1, 2026This paper presents provable randomized algorithms for the exact shortest vector problem (SVP) and the 5/3-approximate closest vector problem (CVP) in the Euclidean norm on random q-ary lattices, for any integer modulus q. The approach adapts the Howgrave-Graham–Joux representation method to find short ternary solutions of random linear congruences. For density at most 1, both algorithms' time exponents fall below the heuristic sieving exponent of 0.2925. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend the Howgrave-Graham–Joux representation method to all integer moduli, giving provable SVP and CVP algorithms on random q-ary lattices with time exponents below sieving.

entry.title: A Compiler Keeping Computations Secure Under Constant Continual Memory Leakage
entry.summary: A Constant-Rate Compiler for Continual Memory Leakage IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper presents a compiler that transforms any deterministic computation so that physical leakage from its implementation reveals nothing beyond its input-output behaviour, under the continual memory leakage model. It achieves constant leakage-rate, whereas previous general compilers tolerated only inverse-polynomial leakage-rate. Applied to decryption of IND-CCA2 secure public-key encryption, it yields IND-CCLA2 security, instantiated from LWE and LPN, and the authors also obtain signatures, PRFs and MACs via a generalization. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a constant-leakage-rate compiler in the continual memory leakage model, improving prior inverse-polynomial rates, with applications to PKE, signatures and PRFs.

entry.title: Tightly Secure Unique Signatures in the Random Oracle Model via Hash-and-Subset-Sign
entry.summary: Unique Signature Schemes with Tight Security in the Random Oracle Model via Hash-and-Subset-Sign IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies unique signature schemes, in which each message has exactly one valid signature. Most such schemes previously suffered a security loss at least linear in the number of signature queries under EUF-CMA security. The authors give a hash-and-sign-like general transformation that turns a scheme with weaker security into an EUF-CMA secure one. The result is the first tightly secure unique signature scheme with verifiable public keys that needs only a constant number (six) of random oracle queries to sign and verify. The paper also gives two tightly secure constructions in the multi-user setting. ★★★★ Notable: The authors give a hash-and-subset-sign transformation yielding the first tight unique signature with verifiable keys using constant oracle queries, plus multi-user constructions.

entry.title: Concrete distance bounds for accumulate error-correcting codes over fixed finite fields
entry.summary: Concrete Minimum Distance Bounds of Accumulate Codes over any Fixed Finite Field IACR ePrint · Nov 1, 2026This paper analyzes the minimum distance of three accumulate-type error-correcting codes, Repeat-Accumulate, Repeat-Accumulate-Accumulate, and Expand-Accumulate, over any finite field. It gives explicit closed-form upper bounds on the probability that each code fails to reach a target relative minimum distance, using a new fine-grained union bound. Numerical examples show the RA code has very small distance, while RAA and EA codes achieve larger distances over smaller fields.

entry.title: CHAMP at the Bit: Short Square-Root Collisions for Cayley Hashes
entry.summary: CHAMPing at the Bit: Short Square-Root Collisions for Two-Generator Cayley Hashes IACR ePrint · Nov 1, 2026This paper studies collisions in two-generator Cayley hashes (CHAMP) built from two matrices over a prime field. The authors construct collisions by finding two palindromes whose matrix products commute, yielding collisions of 4⌈log₂(p+3)⌉ bits. Under a uniformity heuristic, such pairs can be found after about √(πp/2) class evaluations. They argue that no pair of generators gives a 2×2 Cayley hash over a prime field with collision resistance greater than O(√p).

entry.title: Batch accumulators for zero-knowledge membership proofs in large-scale onboarding
entry.summary: Polynomial Batch Accumulators for Onboarding-Dominant Zero-Knowledge Membership Proofs IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper introduces Polynomial Equation Batching (PEB), a zero-knowledge membership accumulator designed for workloads dominated by enrolling large member rosters. Each batch of up to 128 members is represented as a characteristic polynomial whose coefficients are hashed with Poseidon, and batches run in parallel to scale to large populations. Two variants are described: PEB-A maps secrets directly to polynomial roots, and PEB-B hashes secrets inside the circuit. The authors report that PEB-A achieves up to a 149.07x mean speedup in per-user initialization versus incremental Merkle trees, with a 33.87% proof-generation overhead.

entry.title: Key recovery attack on RLCE using the GIJS distinguisher
entry.summary: Key Recovery Against RLCE via the GIJS Distinguisher IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper presents an experimental cryptanalysis of the RLCE cryptosystem at the parameter regime w=n-k, previously considered secure. The attack relies on the recent GIJS distinguisher, shortening the public key and running it with each column as hold-out to identify twin column pairs. The authors report breaking the ID-0 (128-bit) parameter set in about 30.5 core-hours (roughly 3 hours wall time) on a standard higher-end laptop.

entry.title: Rechecking accountability in accountable tracing signatures, a cryptographic signature type.
entry.summary: Revisiting Accountability in Accountable Tracing Signatures IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026Accountable tracing signatures classify group members as traceable or non-traceable. The paper formalizes accountability soundness, requiring that no two witnesses certify the same user as both traceable and non-traceable. It shows the Kohlweiss-Miers scheme violates this property and proposes a patched version. The authors also discuss applying the attack to lattice-based and isogeny-based schemes.

entry.title: Minimum-latency 5-bit APN S-box construction and classification
entry.summary: Construction and Classification of Minimum-Latency 5-Bit APN S-Boxes IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper studies building and classifying minimum-latency 5-bit APN (almost perfect nonlinear) permutation S-boxes under a prescribed gate-delay model, using exact minimum latencies of Boolean component functions. Under the NanGate 45nm standard cell library's fixed gate-delay model, the authors build a minimum-latency database covering all 5-input balanced nonlinear Boolean functions. They establish a minimum latency of 126.745ps over all 5-bit APN permutations and give explicit constructions attaining it. Compared with selected 5-bit S-box implementations, latency decreases by 10.20%–29.18% and normalized gate area by 5.37%–27.69%.

entry.title: Outsourced Incrementally Verifiable MPC: a framework letting outside parties efficiently verify long-running multiparty computation
entry.summary: Authenticated Outsourced Incrementally Verifiable MPC IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper proposes IV-MPC, a framework for publicly verifiable long-running multiparty computation. It separates private proof computation done by MPC nodes from public proof tasks that can be delegated to a single external prover. The framework combines a private-opening polynomial commitment scheme, a distributed proof system based on sumcheck and compressed Σ-protocols, and a stateless handover technique that anchors committee transfers to a fixed state commitment. External auditors can thus verify correctness at every round, with verification time asymptotically independent of the total number of epochs.

entry.title: Normal-Jet Masking: A Retraining-Free Defense Against Neural Network Extraction Attacks
entry.summary: Normal-Jet Masking: A Retraining-Free Defense Against Cryptanalytic Extraction of Neural Networks IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper proposes Normal-Jet Masking (NJM), a post-training wrapper that defends piecewise-linear neural networks against cryptanalytic extraction without changing the source model. NJM sets a tangent–normal tube around protected data, keeps private normal-direction mask channels inactive inside it, and mixes their activations into served outputs outside it. Across seven MLPs, the authors report that NJM reduces raw-logit evidence F1 by 53.8–93.1%, raises query cost by 1.4–9.3×, and eliminates pure hard-label duals. On CNNs, it keeps agreement at least 0.9993.

entry.title: Distill and Conquer: Extracting Local Rules from Hidden Neural Networks Using Only Hard Labels
entry.summary: Distill and Conquer: Cryptanalytic Extraction of Local Rules in the Hard-Label Setting IACR ePrint · Nov 2, 2026This paper proposes Distill–Probe–Extract, a method that extracts explicit local class-pair rules from a neural network using only hard-label queries, without first identifying the victim's architecture. Verified boundary events train a student model whose gradients propose boundary directions that are refined through victim queries. The extracted rules are then tested with fresh hard-label queries. Experiments cover digit multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, Fashion-MNIST, and trained Blended watermarks.

entry.title: Beyond Standard Indifferentiability: Simulator Properties for Fiat-Shamir Security
entry.summary: Beyond Standard Indifferentiability: Simulator Properties for Fiat-Shamir Security IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies how to replace the random oracle in the Fiat-Shamir transform with structured hash constructions while preserving security. It shows that standard indifferentiability can still serve as the oracle-replacement abstraction, giving generic transfer theorems for three knowledge-soundness extraction interfaces. It also argues that the reconstruction requirement for rewinding extraction is inherent, and instantiates the framework for tagged prefix-free Merkle-Damgard and a fixed-output permutation sponge. ★★★★ Notable: Addresses the Chiesa-Orru gap by showing standard indifferentiability suffices as an oracle-replacement abstraction, with generic transfer theorems and a rewinding-reconstruction lower bound under dis

entry.title: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Limits of Masked-Code Encryption
entry.summary: Hidden Curves and Short Duals: Cubic Jets, Dual Leaks, and the Limits of Masked-Code Encryption IACR ePrint · Nov 1, 2026This paper analyzes two masking schemes, Wang's RLCE and the (U|U+V) construction of UVW-KEM, which were proposed as compact alternatives to Goppa codes. The authors show that for Reed-Solomon and algebraic-geometry codes the mask hides a curve, which can be detected through cubic jet counts, and they explain a public-key key recovery attack on UVW-KEM that is not specific to UVW. They also show that both masks preserve the dual of the hidden code, leaking low-weight dual words. The authors conclude that no compact masked trapdoor code is currently known that avoids these structural weaknesses. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors propose hidden-pairing codes, give a closed-form cubic jet dependency bound, and report that both masks leak the hidden code's dual across parameters.

entry.title: Poly versus Polyval: comparing polynomial-evaluation hash functions
entry.summary: Poly Versus Polyval IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper revisits Poly, a polynomial-evaluation hash function over binary extension fields GF(2^n) with n=64k and k≥2. Unlike GHASH, it avoids per-block bit reversals and is faster, and it differs from the faster Polyval by using usual rather than Montgomery reduction. The authors give algorithms with correctness proofs and optimised assembly implementations for n=128, 256 and 512. They report that Polyval is faster for n=128, while Poly is faster for n=256 and larger.

entry.title: TxBench: A Benchmark of Attack Transactions and Evidence-Backed Negatives on Seven EVM Chains
entry.summary: TxBench: A Benchmark of Attack Transactions and Evidence-Backed Negatives on Seven EVM Chains arXiv · Nov 3, 2026TxBench is a benchmark for testing detectors of malicious smart-contract transactions, covering seven EVM chains. Its attack transactions come from cited incidents in BlockSec's library and the EVM Hack Registry, filtered by a five-step pipeline that rebuilds each transaction's execution, and its negatives are ordinary chain transactions confirmed as legitimate. Of 1,850 cited transactions, 1,012 attacks from 602 incidents were accepted. Four zero-shot LLMs were precise but detected at most 0.43 of the attacks and no key compromises. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present a benchmark of EVM attack transactions labeled by their own execution, with evidence-backed negatives; the summary reports 1,012 accepted attacks from 1,850 cited transactions, che

entry.title: Information Loss Is All You Need: Post-Quantum TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices
entry.summary: Information Loss Is All You Need: TC⁰ Pseudorandomness from Worst-Case Lattices arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper introduces learning with algebraic rounding (LAR), which applies deterministic integer rounding to blocks of secret-dependent linear measurements and encodes the result in a lattice quotient. For a fixed family with polynomially bounded modulus and dimensions, the authors show these deterministic labels on uniform, secret-independent public matrices are computationally indistinguishable from uniform labels given any polynomial number of classical random examples. Security rests on quantum worst-case hardness of GapSVP and SIVP over general lattices at approximation factor Õ(q). The construction yields a post-quantum weak pseudorandom function with joint key-and-input evaluation in TC⁰, and the paper also proves hardness of learning polynomial-size two-hidden-layer ReLU networks from noiseless uniform random examples. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose learning with algebraic rounding, a deterministic-rounding construction giving a TC0 weak PRF from worst-case lattice hardness, plus ReLU network learning hardness.

entry.title: Interactive Privacy Boosts Accuracy in Edge-Private Subgraph Counting
entry.summary: The Power of Interaction in Locally Edge-Private Subgraph Counting arXiv · Nov 4, 2026This paper studies counting subgraphs of a fixed pattern in any undirected graph under interactive local edge differential privacy. The authors propose a two-round algorithm, Linear Noise Cancellation, with error O(n^{k-3/2}/ε^ℓ) on every graph, showing that one extra interaction round can polynomially improve worst-case accuracy over noninteractive methods. They also give a Predict and Correct framework for graphs with bounded maximum degree and prove matching lower bounds in n and d. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a two-round interactive method improving triangle counting error by √n, with matching lower bounds showing tight bounds.

entry.title: Leakage-resilient computation through matrix refreshing: a way to protect secrets from side-channel leaks
entry.summary: Leakage-Resilient Computation via Matrix Refreshing arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies cryptographic methods that keep secrets safe even when side-channel attacks reveal partial information about a device's internal state. A secret is split into two shares held by separate parties, and each refresh multiplies one share by an invertible matrix and the other by its inverse. The authors prove this refresh remains secure under continual local leakage and give explicit bounds on statistical distance. They also present a circuit compiler supporting repeated stateful computation, along with efficient simulation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show matrix refreshing of inner-product shares resists continual local leakage, with bounds for refreshes, a circuit compiler, and simulation.

entry.title: BrainwashedLLM: Jailbreaking Large Reasoning Models by Automatically Discovering Adversarial Chains of Thought
entry.summary: BrainwashedLLM: Jailbreaking via Automated Adversarial Chain of Thoughts Discovery arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines the safety risks of the explicit chain-of-thought reasoning produced by Large Reasoning Models, showing that the reasoning trace itself can serve as an attack vector. The authors propose BrainwashedLLM, which uses reinforcement learning (GRPO) to train a small white-box model to generate adversarial reasoning traces, then injects these traces as prefixes into larger black-box reasoning models. The method reportedly achieves ASR@5 between 0.74 and 0.98 across four state-of-the-art models without querying the target during attack construction. The authors argue that exposed chain-of-thought is a vulnerability and suggest architectural defenses such as isolating the reasoning buffer. ★★★★ Notable: The authors use RL to optimize a small model's reasoning traces as an attack surface, transferring them zero-shot; the abstract reports ASR@5 across four large reasoning models.

entry.title: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warnings Used to Steer AI Agents
entry.summary: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper shows that attackers can manipulate LLM agents by exploiting their own harm-avoidance behavior. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, causes the agent to rule out legitimate options and choose the attacker's target, without any injected command. Tests across six models and ten consumer-service domains found this steers agents about as often as instruction injection while evading injection detectors. Adding a corroboration requirement to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose steering agents via their own harm avoidance, report tests across six models and ten domains, and evaluate a mitigation.

entry.title: Gaussian difference dynamics: classical randomized algorithms that beat the 2^{n/2} barrier for lattice sampling and shortest vectors
entry.summary: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the 2ⁿ/2 Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper presents classical randomized algorithms that break the 2^{n/2} time barrier for discrete Gaussian sampling and the Shortest Vector Problem on lattices. It introduces Gaussian difference dynamics, a framework that tracks expected vector counts and pairwise clustering through repeated differencing. The authors also address batch sampling and answer a question of Stephens-Davidowitz about centered sampling. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce Gaussian difference dynamics and report discrete Gaussian sampling in (3/2)^{n/2} time on arbitrary lattices, breaking the 2^{n/2} barrier.

entry.title: Can harmless skills make LLM agents behave unsafely?
entry.summary: Can Benign Skills Induce Misaligned Behavior in LLM Agents? arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies whether adding reusable benign skills to LLM agents can lead them to take external actions that violate safety requirements. Comparing agents with and without skills across five LLM backbones and three benchmarks, the authors find that skills raise benign task accuracy by 10.3 percentage points on average but also raise the unsafe action rate by 10.3 points. The paper also examines factors that worsen this risk and shows that a guard checking tool actions before execution reduces violations while keeping gains on benign tasks. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors identify skill-induced misalignment, comparing agents with and without benign skills across five backbones and three benchmarks, and test a pre-execution guard.

entry.title: "The Native Menace": Host-to-Browser Cross-Boundary Attacks via Native Messaging
entry.summary: The Native Menace: Host-to-Browser Cross-Boundary Attacks via Native Messaging arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents the first empirical security analysis of the browser NativeMessaging API, which lets extensions communicate with native apps on a user's machine. The authors describe a novel attack in which a non-privileged malicious native app misuses this channel to stealthily intercept sensitive communications or launch confused deputy attacks against other native apps. They demonstrate concrete attacks against popular apps and their browser extensions. The paper also proposes mitigating these attacks with message encryption using out-of-band secret sharing. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors present the first security analysis of native messaging, demonstrating attacks on 1Password and government signing workflows, and propose encrypted messages with out-of-band secret sharing

entry.title: A paper showing that quantum advantage has limited complexity implications
entry.summary: Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications arXiv · Nov 4, 2026The paper examines the complexity-theoretic consequences of proofs of quantumness and quantum-verifier oblivious state preparation. The authors give oracle evidence that both can exist even when P = NP or BQP = QCMA. Their oracle separations lead to conclusions about what relativizing proofs can and cannot establish for classical or quantum cryptography.

entry.title: Leftover Attribute Leakage Depends on Evaluation Setup: Auditing Privacy Tests After Text Anonymization
entry.summary: Residual Attribute Leakage Is an Interface: Auditing Privacy Evaluation After Text De-identification arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies how privacy is measured for de-identified text, where a language model tries to guess a protected attribute of a person. It defines a prior-normalised, clipped leakage score for the gain in confidence on the true value. Varying the evaluation setup on fixed releases of three corpora changes the conclusions drawn. The authors also build a traceable editor, SACC, as an experimental tool and use ablations to show where its advantage does not hold.

entry.title: Extracting LLM system prompts from complex agent settings using hierarchical optimization
entry.summary: Extracting System Prompt of LLM Services in Complex (Agentic) Settings: Hierarchical Optimization and Reliable Evaluation Metrics arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the leakage of system prompts, a valuable intellectual property of large language model services. The authors show that existing prompt extraction attacks perform poorly on newer services with longer, more structured prompts and where only post-processed outputs are visible. They propose ExtraHerO, which decomposes extraction into hierarchical reconstruction guided by a structural template and iteratively refines adversarial queries. Experiments report consistent gains over prior methods on chatbots and agents.

entry.title: Correct tool, wrong parameters: defending LLM agents against parameter poisoning
entry.summary: Right Tool, Wrong Parameters: Defending LLM Agents Against Parameter Poisoning arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper studies a stealthier attack on LLM agents in which an attacker keeps the intended action but manipulates tool arguments, such as a recipient. It proposes AuthorityFlow, a three-stage defense that builds a task-specific trust hierarchy over information fields, traces where each argument value comes from, and accepts changes only from fields trusted to set that parameter. The authors also introduce the FactAuthBench benchmark. The attack success rate drops from 93.06% without defense to 9.03%, while benign task utility is 82.64% versus 90.28% without defense.

entry.title: Nine Dimensions for Classifying Prompt Injection Attacks
entry.summary: The Devil is in the Context: Nine Dimensions of Prompt Injection Attacks arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper argues that prompt injection attacks differ widely and are usually evaluated as one homogeneous type. It proposes a taxonomy of nine dimensions describing the injected instruction, its relation to the user's task, and how it appears in the target system. The authors apply it to six real-world vulnerabilities and nine existing benchmarks, finding that most benchmarks cover only a small part of this space and that 13% of pairwise category combinations remain untested.

entry.title: VeriSpoof: Going Beyond Real-or-Fake Speech Detection with One Audio LLM
entry.summary: VeriSpoof: Beyond Real or Fake with One Audio LLM arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents VeriSpoof, an audio language model that uses shared weights to handle five tasks: deepfake detection, generator attribution, recording-condition analysis, synthesized-span localisation, and source verification. Each decision comes with rationales whose statements can be independently checked. The authors release two models, inference code, a demo, and the VeriSpoof-Bench evaluation suite.

entry.title: Perseus: a full-stack system that runs AI models on encrypted data
entry.summary: Perseus: A Full-Stack System for Homomorphic Model Inference arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents Perseus, a free and open Python library for running machine learning models on encrypted data using fully homomorphic encryption. It covers the whole stack, from the cryptographic backend and data packing to encrypted nonlinear operations and end-to-end model execution, with an optimization added at each level. Perseus reports state-of-the-art latency across several models and stays within 3% of plaintext models' accuracy and perplexity.

entry.title: Security analysis of verifiable credential verification pipelines, comparing JSON-LD/RDFC canonicalization with SD-JWT VC and mdoc
entry.summary: A Security Analysis of Verifiable Credential Verification Pipelines: Attack Surface Arising from JSON-LD/RDFC Canonicalization Compared with SD-JWT VC and mdoc arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper examines the implemented verification pipelines of three verifiable credential formats: SD-JWT VC, the W3C VCDM 2.0 with the eddsa-rdfc-2022 cryptosuite, and mdoc. For the W3C format, it tests attacks arising from remote context resolution and RDFC-1.0 canonicalization, including denial of service via poison graphs, context injection through @context, and server-side request forgery. The authors report that suitable mitigations include a static document loader, a context allowlist, and a call limit with a size bound. SD-JWT VC and mdoc resisted every attack vector evaluated.

entry.title: Averaging attacks by colluding users break traceability in personalized neural audio watermarks
entry.summary: Averaging Collusion Breaks Traceability in Personalized Neural Audio Watermarking arXiv · Nov 3, 2026Personalized neural audio watermarks embed user-specific payloads so a leaked copy can be traced to its recipient. The paper finds that averaging just two copies sample-by-sample causes tracing failures in 87.7% to 99.7% of cases across five systems while keeping audio quality largely intact. In a payload-aware setting, adjusting mixture weights can steer the decoder toward a chosen nonmember, and a confidence screen rejects many collusion-induced assignments.

entry.title: CloakFEM: Agent-Based FEM Code Generation for Testing Computational Resource Exhaustion
entry.summary: CloakFEM: Agentic FEM Code Generation for Red-Teaming Computational Resource Exhaustion arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents CloakFEM, an LLM-agent framework that automatically generates runnable adversarial finite element method (FEM) programs that amplify solver computation. It combines LLM-guided search, an FEM-specific intermediate representation, and a deterministic validity check. In experiments across three FEM stacks, 17 problem classes, and 1,068 seeds, solver iterations rose from 43 to 247,367, a 5,752.72-fold amplification, while inputs remained valid and solvable.

entry.title: Two-sided protection for private LoRA inference using Intel TDX
entry.summary: Bilateral Protection for Private LoRA Inference with Intel TDX arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents a system that uses Intel Trust Domain Extensions (TDX) to protect both client inputs and proprietary LoRA adapter parameters during inference. The client and the LoRA owner each verify remote attestation and TLS key binding before releasing their secrets. Experiments show protected inference produces identical token sequences to native CPU inference across 400 dialogues, with a steady-state time ratio of about 1.0094.

entry.title: How group debate between AI agents can amplify web safety risks
entry.summary: When Debate Amplifies Risk: Social-Bias Vulnerabilities in Multi-Agent Safety Deliberation arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies multi-agent debate systems that use retrieved web content, testing whether social pressures such as conformity and deference to authority can make AI agents accept unsafe advice when sources mix safe and risky information. The authors introduce SafeConflict-Bias, a controlled diagnostic protocol covering six web risk categories that holds queries and evidence fixed while varying majority opinion, authority cues, and confidence. Standard debate raised unsafe adoption from 0.0% to 100.0% and suppressed safe minority evidence. The proposed RiskTrace-Debias framework, an inference-time auditing method, limits worst-case unsafe adoption to 2.0% or less without causing over-refusal.

entry.title: VerfGraph: An Efficient Zero-Knowledge System for Verifiable Graph Queries
entry.summary: VerfGraph: Efficient Zero-Knowledge Verifiable Graph Query Evaluation System arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents VerfGraph, a zero-knowledge system that lets a client verify that a graph query was correctly evaluated over committed private graph data, without revealing private records or intermediate values. It builds on the expansion-centric model of ZKGraph and adds new operator-proof methods for expansion and shortest-path operations, along with correctness proofs for count and weighted shortest-path operators. On the LDBC Social Network Benchmark, compared with ZKGraph on complex IC queries, VerfGraph achieves 33.9 to 59.7 times faster proof generation and 4.5 to 6.6 times lower peak prover memory.

entry.title: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: New Algorithms for Shortest Vector and Discrete Gaussian Sampling
entry.summary: Gaussian Difference Dynamics: Breaking the 2ⁿ/2 Barrier for the Shortest Vector Problem and Discrete Gaussian Sampling IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper presents classical randomized algorithms that break the 2^{n/2} barrier for discrete Gaussian sampling and the Shortest Vector Problem in lattices. It introduces Gaussian difference dynamics, a framework that tracks expected counts and pairwise clustering of vectors through repeated differencing. The approach uses thin spherical shells and a double rejection technique to control the distribution of batch samples. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors introduce Gaussian difference dynamics and report new exponents breaking the 2^{n/2} barrier for SVP and discrete Gaussian sampling.

entry.title: Quantum time-space tradeoffs for short Merkle-Damgård collisions
entry.summary: Quantum Time-Space Tradeoffs for Short Merkle-Damgård Collisions IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper studies how much time and quantum memory an attacker needs to find short collisions in Merkle-Damgård hashing, under a quantum auxiliary-input random-oracle model. It introduces a structure-sensitive compressed-oracle analysis that yields tighter bounds, including a tight characterization for two-block collisions even against arbitrary quantum advice. The authors also propose the ST²B conjecture for the correct constant-success tradeoff. ★★★★ Notable: The authors develop a structure-sensitive compressed-oracle analysis, giving a tight bound for two-block collisions and resolving an open problem.

entry.title: Short collisions show Sponge and Merkle-Damgård hash designs differ under preprocessing
entry.summary: Short Collisions Separate Sponge from Merkle-Damgård IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper studies short collisions in salted Merkle-Damgård and Sponge hash constructions under a query-bounded preprocessing model. With identical query budgets, the authors show Sponge admits constant-probability collisions using only three message blocks, while Merkle-Damgård adversaries with B = o(T₂) blocks succeed with probability o(1). The results show that collision length interacts differently with preprocessing in the two constructions. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show Sponge and Merkle-Damgård separate under query-bounded preprocessing via short collisions, reporting a three-block Sponge attack and a matching MD upper bound.

entry.title: A statistical model for ratio-based ring oscillator PUFs
entry.summary: Ratio-Based Ring Oscillator PUF Statistical Model IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper presents a mathematically derived closed-form statistical model that describes the counter value distribution of ratio-based ring oscillator physical unclonable functions (ROPUFs). The authors validate the model's assumptions using ring oscillator measurements from 218 Xilinx Artix-7 FPGAs. The model allows theoretical quantification of response entropy and enables advanced bit derivation methods, such as Equiprobable Quantization and Two-Metric Helper Data, which achieve better reliability, randomness, and bit yield than the original counter-based derivation. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose a closed-form statistical model of counter distributions for ratio-based ROPUFs, enabling entropy quantification and new bit derivation methods, validated on 218 FPGAs.

entry.title: Authentication complexity of Byzantine consensus: how much initial key authentication is needed to tolerate faulty parties
entry.summary: The Authentication Complexity of Byzantine Consensus IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies how much initial authentication distributed parties need to reach Byzantine broadcast and agreement despite faulty parties. Each party's public verification key is authenticated only to a chosen subset of others, modeled by a directed authentication graph. The authors define authentication complexity as the minimum number of such bindings and give a tight graph characterization of setups that support agreement. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose authentication complexity and give a tight graph characterization of initial authentication setups supporting Byzantine agreement.

entry.title: Machine-Checked Soundness Proof of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates
entry.summary: Soundness of the GKR Protocol for Sparse-Merkle Updates, with a Machine-Checked Core arXiv · Oct 5, 2026This paper machine-checks in Isabelle/HOL the soundness of the GKR protocol for sparse-Merkle membership, non-membership and update proofs, together with arithmetization exactness and leaf-commitment binding. It proves that for a false output claim, the probability that a layered sumcheck accepts a false result is at most (s_out + Σ(2 s_i d_i + 1))/|F|. The bound is instantiated over a quartic extension of the 31-bit KoalaBear field, giving a denominator of about 2^124. The model covers only the interactive public-coin protocol and excludes Fiat-Shamir, knowledge soundness and zero knowledge.

entry.title: Secret sharing without extractable randomness
entry.summary: Secret Sharing Despite Non-Extractable Randomness arXiv · Oct 14, 2026This paper studies the randomness needed for two-out-of-two secret sharing. Bosley and Dodis asked in 2007 whether such schemes must also allow deterministic extraction of nearly uniform bits from the randomness source. The authors answer no: for each b≥2, they build a class of flat sources with min-entropy at least b and a perfectly correct, perfectly private scheme that splits a b-bit secret into two (b+1)-bit shares. The idea is extended to other threshold settings. ★★★★ Notable: A parity-based counterexample answers Bosley and Dodis's open question negatively for two-out-of-two secret sharing and extends the construction to two-out-of-n and r-out-of-r thresholds.

entry.title: Path-Finding and State Preparation in the Security of Invariant Quantum Money
entry.summary: Anchoring the Security of Invariant Quantum Money arXiv · Sep 30, 2026This paper examines the assumptions underlying the security of quantum money based on knots and invariant money. Existing proofs rely on additional knowledge-of-path assumptions whose relation to security is unclear. When equivalence classes are orbits of efficiently computable group actions, average-case hardness of path-finding is shown to be necessary for security. For knots, forgery reduces only to an equally hard state-preparation problem, and the authors propose a falsifiable preparation assumption equivalent to security. ★★★★ Notable: The paper proposes a state-preparation assumption in place of path-finding and argues their combination is equivalent to security.

entry.title: Penalty deposits that let a trusted party stake its own discrete-log secrets, with zero-knowledge proofs to show the stake
entry.summary: Penalty Deposits For Discrete Logarithms IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper proposes a technique that lets a trusted party in a protocol attach deposits to its own secrets without weakening security, and prove this to others with zero-knowledge proofs. If the party compromises the protocol by error or by revealing its secrets, the attached deposit goes to attackers. The authors formalize the technique and its security notions, give two practical constructions in generic discrete logarithm groups, and analyze its use in ECDLP-based protocols.

entry.title: Elliptic curve arithmetic for quantum attacks on Curve25519
entry.summary: Elliptic Curve Arithmetic for Quantum Cryptanalysis: A Study of Curve25519 IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper implements modern affine circuit techniques on the Curve25519 elliptic curve for quantum cryptanalysis. It obtains a scalar circuit using 47,199,530 CCX gates and 1,189 peak logical qubits, about 18% fewer gates and 35% fewer qubits than Schrottenloher's secp256k1 circuits. The authors present three contributions: established arithmetic and signed table techniques, odd signed digit recoding for quantum windows, and an exception-free addition schedule using a fixed 8-torsion offset point.

entry.title: Weir: a memory-bounded indexing and proof protocol using sequential storage
entry.summary: Weir: Bounded-Memory Indexing and Proving with Sequential Storage IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026The paper presents Weir, a Shockwave-derived protocol that performs read-write indexing and proving under bounded prover memory. Under an external-query-tape model, it uses O(B+log T) field RAM, constant digest RAM and polylogarithmic auxiliary RAM. A fused Split-Butterfly-Merge removes n-1 materialized transform passes at length 2^n. In a fixed 64 MiB worker-cap grid, the RW schedule completes all tested matrix and Poseidon inputs, while the RAM prover completes only matrix dimension 8.

entry.title: Re-examining Hash-ECB-Hash encryption: plaintext recovery attacks on PEP and TET
entry.summary: Revisiting Hash-ECB-Hash Enciphering: Plaintext Recovery Attacks on PEP and TET IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026The paper revisits two Hash-ECB-Hash tweakable enciphering schemes, PEP (FSE 2006) and TET (CRYPTO 2007), which encrypt whole multi-block data units without length expansion. For PEP, it exhibits a fixed public field satisfying the published parameter rule whose position coefficients repeat, enabling a two-query distinguisher and recovery of a secret tweak-derived value. For TET, it analyzes two corrections of a reported encryption/decryption mismatch and shows two-query distinguishers on messages with a partial final block, plus deterministic plaintext recovery for tails of at least two bits.

entry.title: Faster implementations of small-modulus lattice KEM components
entry.summary: Efficient Implementations of Small-Modulus Lattice KEM Components IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper optimizes lattice-based key encapsulation components that use small moduli 257 and 769, covering encoding, uniform public polynomial generation, and polynomial multiplication. It introduces zero-selector encoding for modulus 257 and specialized rejection sampling for modulus 769. The optimizations are integrated into the BAT and END schemes, with reported reductions in encapsulation and decapsulation costs.

entry.title: Batched encryption tied to identities, with one short proof that chosen ciphertexts were deleted
entry.summary: Batched Identity-Based Encryption with Succinct Publicly Verifiable Subset Deletion IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper introduces batched identity-based encryption with succinct publicly verifiable subset deletion (BIBE-SPVD). Holders of many quantum ciphertexts can prove that any chosen subset was deleted using one short classical certificate, while the remaining ciphertexts stay usable. The aggregate certificate size is poly(λ, log N), independent of how many ciphertexts are deleted.

entry.title: Batched threshold predicate encryption built on succinct LWE
entry.summary: Batched Threshold Predicate Encryption from Succinct LWE IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper introduces batched threshold predicate encryption (BT-PE), which combines batch-scoped authorization, predicate-based access control, and threshold decryption. The authors give a lattice-based construction that supports polynomial-size arithmetic-circuit predicates, compact batch digests, and compact per-party key shares. Decryption requires that the encrypted attribute belongs to the authorized batch, satisfies the required predicate, and enough parties participate. Correctness and query-selective one-sided security are proven under the ℓ-succinct LWE assumption.

entry.title: Registered functional encryption with proof of permanent data deletion
entry.summary: Registered Functional Encryption with Certified Everlasting Security IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026Registered functional encryption lets users register their own public keys without a trusted authority. Certified everlasting deletion lets a recipient issue a classical certificate showing a ciphertext has been destroyed in an information-theoretic sense. This paper combines the two for the first time, defining the scheme's syntax and security and giving a construction based on pseudorandom and authenticated BB84 encodings.

entry.title: Practical Collision Attacks on Reduced-Step SM3
entry.summary: Practical Collision Attacks on 22- and 23-Step SM3 (Preliminary Version) IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper presents practical collisions for 22-step and 23-step versions of the SM3 hash function, using the standard initial value. These results extend the 20-step collision of Mendel et al. (2013) by two and three steps, respectively. The time complexities are about 2^52.4 and 2^54.5 evaluations of the respective reduced-step SM3. The authors also give a semi-free-start collision for 24-step SM3.

entry.title: SPIDER: A Faster, Smaller Identity-Based Signature from Isogenies
entry.summary: SPIDER: A Faster and Smaller Identity-Based Signature From Isogenies IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper presents SPIDER, a digital signature built on a sigma protocol that proves knowledge of an isogeny of prime or non-smooth degree from a supersingular elliptic curve, so it can be seen as a proof of knowledge of a PRISM signature. Combining SPIDER with PRISM yields an identity-based signature scheme called SPIDER-IBS. The authors state it is the most efficient and compact isogeny-based identity-based signature.

entry.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight Through Rewinding
entry.summary: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper addresses how a weak verifier can check the outputs of more powerful AI systems, introducing rewindable interactive proofs (RIPs), in which the verifier can roll the prover back to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. The authors construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. The construction uses no cryptography and is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover.

entry.title: Card-based protocols mixing one- and two-card encodings, and the fewest cards needed
entry.summary: Card-Based Protocols with Mixed Encoding: Computable Functions and the Minimum Number of Cards IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper studies card-based secure computation in which one player commits a bit with a single card and the other with two cards. It characterizes which functions can be computed this way, including AND but not XOR. The authors prove that Mizuki's five-card AND protocol is card-minimal and verify the lower bound with QBF solvers.

entry.title: SpreadMAYO: Faster GPU Signatures via Greater Parallelism for MAYO
entry.summary: SpreadMAYO: Unlocking Greater Parallelism for Faster MAYO Signatures on GPUs IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026This paper presents SpreadMAYO, a high-throughput GPU implementation of MAYO, a multivariate post-quantum signature scheme that is a Round 3 candidate in NIST's additional signature process. It uses finer task partitioning and a revised signing pipeline to expose more parallelism and reduce thread synchronization. On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, it reports speedups of 2.33–3.71× for key generation, 4.40–6.93× for signing, and 3.42–5.13× for verification over a Round 3 adapted GPU baseline.

entry.title: Anamorphic Proofs of Knowledge from Prover Randomness (proofs that also secretly prove a hidden claim to a designated checker)
entry.summary: Anamorphic Proofs of Knowledge from Prover Randomness IACR ePrint · Oct 31, 2026The paper introduces anamorphic proofs of knowledge, in which a normal-looking proof publicly certifies its statement while also convincing a designated checker that the prover knows a witness for a separately registered hidden statement. The construction reuses the prover's commitment to its own randomness, adding a secret mask to the hidden witness. Normal verifiers and external observers cannot distinguish the two modes, and the checker learns neither witness. Instantiations are given for random-base Compressed Sigma protocols and Bulletproofs with range aggregation, and three-move protocols are shown unable to support the primitive under local checking.

entry.title: Same words, different actions: diagnosing text-action divergence in reasoning robot models
entry.summary: Say the Same, Act Differently: Diagnosing and Steering Text-Action Divergence in Reasoning VLAs arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies whether visual perturbations can change the physical actions of reasoning vision-language-action models while leaving their generated rationale word-for-word identical. The authors introduce a text-neutral action-subspace (TNAS) diagnostic and test it on the driving model Alpamayo and the manipulation model InstructVLA. Perturbations along this direction shift actions far more than they change text, and TNAS-guided attacks induce new collisions under unchanged rationales. The authors conclude that an unchanged rationale cannot certify a safe action, so monitors must check the predicted action directly. ★★★★ Notable: The authors show visual perturbations can change actions while the rationale stays word-for-word identical, introducing TNAS diagnostic; experiments report on driving and manipulation VLAs.

entry.title: ScrambleMark: Query-free, watermark-agnostic black-box attack that evades speech watermark detection
entry.summary: ScrambleMark: Zero-Query Watermark-Agnostic Black-Box Evasion of Modern Speech Watermarking arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper presents ScrambleMark, a black-box attack that evades speech watermark detection without any queries and without knowing the specific watermarking scheme. Rather than erasing the watermark, it disrupts the structural consistency of the embedded pattern by scrambling harmonic structure, which preserves perceptual quality. The authors report nearly 97% evasion across three commercial platforms and a 4.2/5 human rating, compared with 1.1 to 1.7 for prior attacks. ★★★★ Notable: The authors propose evading watermarks by scrambling harmonic structure rather than erasing it, reporting about 97% evasion on three commercial platforms.

entry.title: Communication complexity of secure multiparty computation using a random oracle, including quantum settings
entry.summary: On the (Quantum) Communication Complexity of Secure MPC from a Random Oracle arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies the communication complexity of secure multiparty computation (MPC) in the random oracle model. It shows that for MPC with preprocessing, a random oracle cannot reduce online communication, which remains bounded below by Ω(|C|·t/(n-t)). For honest majority MPC, it proves an Ω(|C|) communication lower bound and gives a matching construction for degree-2 polynomials, including inner products, when n = O(log λ). The paper also analyzes protocols that use quantum communication. ★★★★ Notable: The authors extend MPC communication lower bounds to the random oracle model, give matching constructions for degree-2 polynomials, and study quantum communication limits.

entry.title: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLMs
entry.summary: Permitted but Unauthorized: Affordance-Induced Delegated-Scope Violations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper studies whether AI agents in multi-agent systems cross their delegated task scope to act on peers' resources under competitive pressure. Tests across eight LLMs in a CI/CD pipeline and a security-operations incident queue found that whether a peer action is listed as an option drives crossings far more than permissions do. Two defenses blocked every crossing, but neither prevented harm done through an authorized action, such as misreporting incident severity.

entry.title: Gather evidence or act now? Belief-level counterfactual labels for deadline-aware incident response in cyber-physical systems
entry.summary: Gather or Act? Belief-Level Counterfactual Labels for Deadline-Aware Incident Response in Cyber-Physical Systems arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper addresses how a defender of an industrial control system should choose between acting immediately on the likeliest fault cause and first gathering evidence to separate look-alike causes before the process nears shutdown. It introduces TE-GvA, a counterfactual decision dataset built on the revised Tennessee Eastman process, with 9,908 decision points from 1,990 simulated incidents. The authors show that belief-level labels, weighted by exact posterior over twin episodes, make gathering the best action far more often in ambiguous cases and yield lower regret than hindsight labels on stress decisions.

entry.title: A new automated fuzzing method for edk2 boot-time components
entry.summary: Towards Effective Fuzzing of EDK2 Components arXiv · Nov 3, 2026The paper presents Metis, an automated technique for fuzzing edk2, the UEFI-based bootloader, by rehosting its boot-time protocols as user-space applications. It mocks protocol dependencies using a Direct-dependency Component Rehosting strategy and generates fuzzing harnesses through a mix of static analysis and LLM-guided synthesis. Evaluated on 60 drivers covering 162 protocols, Metis reaches 73.1% coverage, about 1.7 times that of FuzzUEr, and discovers 137 previously unknown bugs.

entry.title: What Malware Does After Infection: An Empirical Study of 37 Families
entry.summary: What Malware Actually Does: An Empirical Analysis of Post-Infection Behavior Across Malware Families arXiv · Nov 3, 2026This paper analyzes how 37 malware families behave after infection, using dynamic sandbox runs in CAPEv2. It models behavioral traces as heterogeneous graphs and trains a voting ensemble that reaches 94.44% accuracy and an MCC of 0.863. The authors also classify 24 families and produce per-family behavioral fingerprints across registry, network, process, and API activity, along with LLM-generated reports mapped to MITRE ATT&CK.

entry.title: RuntimeTickets: Source-Based Security Obligations for Agent Skills
entry.summary: RuntimeTickets: Source-Grounded Security Obligations for Agent Skills arXiv · Nov 3, 2026Third-party agent skills extend what autonomous agents can do, but malicious skills can hide data leaks or output manipulation within legitimate workflows. The paper introduces RuntimeTickets, a protocol that enforces and audits security requirements while a skill runs, using a language model to propose task-specific obligations and a deterministic runtime gate to check outbound sends. The authors report that across three unmodified agent frameworks it achieved a 0.0% overlook rate and a 0.0% overkill rate, outperforming production scanners and runtime baselines.

entry.title: JevBreak: a study showing decision models can be steered to wrong answers
entry.summary: JevBreak: Your Model, Their Decision arXiv · Nov 2, 2026The paper shows that restricting a model's outputs to a fixed answer set does not prevent an attacker from steering its decision toward a wrong option. It presents Slot Attack, a black-box method that uses only returned label probabilities and appends component-built text to the input. The authors report 32–99% attack success on initially correct decisions and find that accuracy and confidence do not reliably expose this vulnerability.

entry.title: "The Web Doesn't Sit Still": Self-Evolving Adversarial Attacks on Search Agents
entry.summary: The Web Doesn't Sit Still: Adversarial Self-Evolving Attacks on Search Agents arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper examines how LLM-based search agents, which fetch information from the web, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks such as malicious information injection. It notes that existing attacks rely on static, human-written templates. The authors propose a self-evolving framework that jointly optimizes an attacker's strategy and a defender's mitigation, using a Contrastive Rollout Evolutionary Optimization (CREO) method, along with a controlled sandbox and fine-grained vulnerability metrics. Experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks and frontier LLMs show higher attack efficacy than static baselines.

entry.title: LoRA-Patch: A Directional Steering Defense Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters
entry.summary: LoRA-Patch: Defending Against Backdoored LoRA Adapters via Directional Steering arXiv · Nov 2, 2026Third-party LoRA adapters can carry hidden backdoors that keep normal task performance intact while activating malicious behavior under specific triggers, which standard evaluations often miss. This paper proposes LoRA-Patch, a lightweight defense that realigns adapter directions through layer-wise steering without changing the base model weights. Experiments across five backdoor attacks and three models show it mitigates trigger-activated backdoors, outperforms existing baselines, and preserves benign performance. Patches are constructed within 20 seconds for all evaluated models and adapters.

entry.title: Static security analyzers tested over a decade of C/C++ code evolution
entry.summary: Fixed Detectors, Moving Code: How Well Do Static Security Analyzers Hold Up over a Decade of C/C++ Evolution? arXiv · Nov 2, 2026This paper tests whether static application security testing (SAST) tools stay effective over time, using 20,000 vulnerable and fixed C/C++ cases from 1,116 open-source projects spanning 2016 to 2025. It evaluates several releases of CodeQL and Infer, plus one Semgrep configuration. The authors find that F1 scores vary widely, while the ability to separate vulnerable from fixed code stays near chance. They argue that apparent changes in effectiveness may stem from broader alerting and changing analysis coverage rather than only from lost vulnerability detection.

entry.title: InterceptFuzz: Stateful Fuzzing of Single-Process Simulations via Interception
entry.summary: InterceptFuzz: Interception-based Stateful Fuzzing of Single-Process Targets arXiv · Oct 31, 2026This paper presents InterceptFuzz, a middleware that enables stateful fuzzing of single-process targets, such as wireless protocol simulations, using an unmodified stateless AFL++ engine. It records benign packet traffic through a hook in the target and injects fuzzed packets, organizing sequences in a Prefix Tree and deterministically replaying prefixes before mutation. On OpenThread and ns-3, it covers significantly more branches than baselines on OpenThread and ns-3 Wi-Fi, and found seven previously unknown crash signatures in OpenThread.]

entry.title: Provably recovering secrets from integer quotients: improved bounds for nonlinear hidden number problems
entry.summary: Provable Recovery from Integer Quotients: Improved Bounds for Nonlinear Hidden Number Problems IACR ePrint · Oct 30, 2026This paper studies the hidden number problem, which asks whether a secret can be recovered from partial information linked to it by known algebraic relations. For modulus a prime p, the authors extend provable recovery ranges for three nonlinear variants: modular inversion, elliptic-curve, and hidden-multiplier versions, tolerating a larger fraction of unrevealed lower bits.
